answer: Read the CPU temperature from the latest live sample, report it in degrees Celsius with the spike threshold, and say whether it is above the threshold.
Take the current CPU and GPU temperatures from the live sample, name the top processes by CPU from the same sample, and name the culprit of any heat spike event that is still open.

Scan the heat spike events in the window once and report whether there were any, how many, their total time above threshold (by day if the window spans several days), the peak temperature with its time, and the start time and length of the most recent spike; if there were none, say so.
Take the heat spike events that overlap the window, group them by culprit process, group or unit, and rank the culprits by time above threshold and by peak temperature.
Compare the current temperature, or the peak and the heat spike count in the window, with the same figures averaged over the previous recorded days, and report the difference.

Take the heat spike events whose culprit is the named program and the periods when it was a top process, and report the peak and typical temperature during those periods compared with the temperature without it.
Read the fan speed in RPM from the live sample; fan speed is not recorded, so the answer is the list of what ask can answer.
Take the fan speed history in the window; fan speed is not recorded, so the answer is the list of what ask can answer.
Read the overall CPU load and load average from the latest live sample and say whether the load is above the busy threshold.
Report the load average over 1, 5 and 15 minutes against the number of CPU threads, and whether that is busy.
Rank the processes in the latest live sample by CPU use and report the top ones with their percentages.
Check CPU load, memory use, disk busy and network traffic in the latest live sample against their thresholds, name the ones that are saturated, and name the top process for each.

Scan the CPU spike events in the window once and report how many there were, their total time above threshold (by day if the window spans several days), the peak load with its time, and the start time, length and culprit of the most recent spike.

Add up how long the CPU load stayed above the level the question names (the busy threshold when it names none), in the window or now, from the per-second readings and the hourly figures before they begin, with the longest stretch and when.
Take the CPU spike events in the window, group them by culprit process, group or unit, and rank the culprits by total spike time and peak load.
Take every CPU, memory, disk, network and heat spike event that overlaps the window, order them by size, and name each culprit.
Compare the current CPU load, or the CPU spike count and total spike time in the window, with the average of the previous recorded days, and report the difference.
Search the latest live sample for the named program and say whether it is running; if it is, give its PID, CPU use and memory use.
Take the CPU spike events whose culprit is the named program in the window and report the count, the total spike time and the peak load.
Find the most recent spike event, or live sample, in which the named program appears, and report when it was seen.
List the CPU spike events in the window in time order, giving start time, length, peak load and culprit for each.

Count the processes running in the window, or now: the recorder's count of every process, the kernel's own threads included, and the programs proper from the process records at the window's moment, with the most common names.
Read used, free and total memory from the latest live sample, report them in GB and as a percentage, and say whether use is above the pressure threshold.
Rank the processes in the latest live sample by memory use and report the top ones with their sizes.

Scan the memory spike events in the window once and report how many there were, their total time above threshold (by day if the window spans several days), the peak use with its time and culprit, and the time, size and culprit of the most recent spike.
Take the memory spike events in the window, group them by culprit, and rank the culprits by peak size and total spike time.
Compare current memory use, or the memory spike count and peak in the window, with the average over the previous recorded days, and report the difference.
Order the memory spike events and live samples for each process in the window by time, fit the growth in memory size, and report processes whose memory keeps growing.
Read swap used and total from the live sample; swap use is not recorded, so the answer is the list of what ask can answer.
Take swap use in the window: its peak, when, and its average.
List the times the out-of-memory killer (systemd-oomd or the kernel) killed programs in the window: when, which program, and how much memory it held.
Read how busy the disk is and the read and write rates from the latest live sample, and say whether it is above the busy threshold.
Name the culprit of any disk spike event that is still open; if none is open, say the disk is below the busy threshold.

Scan the disk spike events in the window once and report how many there were, their total time above threshold, the peak busy level and transfer rate, and the time, length and culprit of the most recent and the largest spike.
Take the disk spike events in the window, group them by culprit, and rank the culprits by total spike time and peak rate.
Compare current disk activity, or the disk spike count and total spike time in the window, with the average of previous recorded days.
Read free and used space per filesystem; free disk space is not recorded, so the answer is the list of what ask can answer.
Compare free space between snapshots in the window; free disk space is not recorded, so the answer is the list of what ask can answer.
Rank folders by size; disk space use is not recorded, so the answer is the list of what ask can answer.
Report the drives' health: kernel disk errors over the records and the drive temperature; SMART data needs root and is not read.
Read the download and upload rates from the latest live sample and say whether traffic is above the busy threshold.
Whether the internet provider slows down a service; that happens on the provider's side and is not visible here.
reply: I can't tell whether your provider slows down a service: that happens on their side of the line, and this machine only sees its own traffic. I can tell you how much the network moved and when, or whether the Wi-Fi dropped.

answer: Report the IP address of each connected network interface now; the public address is not known without asking a server online.
Report whether the Wi-Fi is connected, to which network, its signal strength and link speed now.
List the times the Wi-Fi connection dropped in the window, apart from disconnects for sleep, and how long each lasted.
Name the culprit of any network spike event that is still open; if none is open, say traffic is below the busy threshold.

Scan the network spike events in the window once and report how many there were, how long they lasted in total, the total data and peak rate, and the time, length, size and culprit of the most recent and the largest spike.
Take the network spike events in the window, group them by culprit, and rank the culprits by data transferred and peak rate.
Count the incoming connections the firewall blocked in the window, by where they came from and what they tried to reach.
List the programs whose first recorded network connection falls in the window, with when and where, and apart from them the programs already seen online that reached new addresses there.
How much data each website, page or connection used; traffic is recorded for the whole machine only, and connections by address, with no byte counts or site names.
reply: I can't say which website used the most: I measure network traffic for the whole machine only, and I keep which addresses each program connected to, without byte counts or website names. I can tell you how much the machine downloaded and uploaded in a window and its busiest moments, or which programs connected out.

answer: Compare current traffic, or the network spike count and data total in the window, with the average of previous recorded days.
Name the culprits of any open network spike events whose upload rate is over the threshold, with their upload rates.
Take the network spike events in the window, keep the upload side, group by culprit, and rank the culprits by data sent.
Add up the upload bytes of the network spike events in the window and report the total and the peak rate.
Check the open and past network spike events in the window for the named program as culprit with upload traffic, and answer yes or no with the amount sent.
Find the most recent network spike event with upload traffic in the window, optionally for a named program, and report its time and size.
Compare the upload total and spike count in the window with the average of previous recorded days and report the difference and any new uploaders.
Find the latest configuration snapshot with package installs or updates, optionally for a named package, and report its time and how many packages changed.

List the package installs, updates and removals in the configuration snapshots in the window, filtered to the named package if one is given, with old and new versions, counts of sessions and packages by day, and a plain 'no changes' when the list is empty.
Look up the named package in the latest configuration snapshot and report its installed version and install or update date.
Find the package updates just before the first crash, unit failure or new spike pattern in the window, and list them as candidate causes with times.

List the config files that changed between the snapshots in the window, filtered to the named file if one is given, with change times, lines added or removed, and the number of snapshots with changes, saying 'no changes' when the list is empty.
Find the latest configuration snapshot in which the named file changed and report its time and the change.
List the crash records in the window, filtered to the named program if one is given, with time, program and signal or reason, plus the count by day, saying 'no crashes' when the list is empty.
Find the latest crash record for the named program, or for any program, and report its time and signal.
Group the crash records in the window by program and rank the programs by crash count.
Take the crash record for the named program and report its signal and reason, along with the spike events, package updates and device changes in the minutes before it.
Compare the crash count in the window with the average of previous recorded periods, or before and after a named update.
Check each boot in the window for an end without a clean shutdown (a hang, power loss or kernel panic), and say which boots ended that way.
Run the trust check on every process in the latest live sample and list those that are unknown or unexpected.
List the programs that were first seen or failed a trust check in the window, with times.
Run the trust check on the named program and report its path, owning package, version, first-seen time, a yes or no verdict, and which parts of the check failed and when.
Find the first and latest times the named program was seen in trust checks, spike events and live samples.
List the commands run as administrator (sudo, pkexec) in the window, with times and the folder they ran in, and say which were refused and why.
Read the battery level from the latest live sample.
Read the charging state from the latest live sample and answer whether the charger is connected and whether the battery is charging.
Estimate time left from the current drain rate; battery drain history is not recorded, so the answer is the list of what ask can answer.
Take the battery level history in the window; battery history is not recorded, so the answer is the list of what ask can answer.
Report design capacity, current full capacity and cycle count; battery health is not recorded, so the answer is the list of what ask can answer.
List the times the machine went to sleep and woke up in the window, in time order, with how long each sleep lasted, and say plainly that it stayed awake when there were none.
Find the latest wake from sleep, or the latest going to sleep, in the window, or in all the records when no time is given, and report its time and how long that sleep lasted.
Add up the time the machine spent asleep in the window, count the separate sleeps, and give the longest one with its start and end.

Find the latest time the charger was plugged in, or unplugged, as the question asks, in the window or in all the records when no time is given, with the battery level then, the change before it and whether it is still so.
Count the times the charger was plugged in, or unplugged, in the window and list when, with the battery level at each and when it changed back.
Find the latest time the lid was closed, or opened, in the window or in all the records when no time is given, and when it changed back.
Count the times the lid was closed, or opened, in the window and list when, with when it changed back.
List the systemd units and autostart entries enabled at boot from the latest configuration snapshot.
List the systemd unit starts, stops and failures in the window, and the units added to or removed from boot between snapshots.
List the systemd units that failed in the window, or are in a failed state now, ranked by failure count.
Check the named unit's records for failure in the window, or its enabled and running state now, and answer yes or no.
Find the latest start or failure record for the named unit and report its time and result.
Count the start, restart and failure records for the named unit or all units in the window.
Report time since the last boot; boot history is not recorded, so the answer is the list of what ask can answer.
Find the latest boot in the boot history; boot and reboot history is not recorded, so the answer is the list of what ask can answer.
Count the boots in the window; boot history is not recorded, so the answer is the list of what ask can answer.
Report boot duration and the slowest units; boot timing is not recorded, so the answer is the list of what ask can answer.
Find the latest time you logged in to the desktop, or out, in the window or in all the records when no time is given, the login screen's own sessions aside, with what happened just before it.
Count the times you logged in to the desktop, or out, in the window and list when, the login screen's own sessions aside.
List the devices in the latest device record and, if a device is named, say whether it is present.
Report whether Bluetooth is on, which paired devices are connected now, and which are paired but not connected.
Report which programs are recording from a microphone right now.
List the device connect and disconnect records in the window, marking devices seen for the first time.
Find the latest connect or disconnect record for the named device and report its time.
Count the connect and disconnect records for the named device in the window and add up the time it was connected.
Whether an external monitor, TV or second screen was connected, when, or for how long; displays are not recorded, only USB devices, serial ports and drives.
reply: I don't record monitors or screens being connected: the device records cover USB devices, serial ports and drives plugged in or out. I can tell you what was plugged in by USB and when, or what the machine was doing (CPU, GPU, heat) at a time.

answer: Find the latest firmware flash record, optionally for a named board, and report its time, board, image and result.

List the firmware flash records in the window with time, board, image and result, give the success and failure counts per board, and say yes or no to whether the latest flash, or every flash in the window, succeeded, with the error for any that failed.
Report the image, build and time of the latest successful flash record for the named board.
Read the GPU temperature from the latest live sample.
Read the GPU load from the latest live sample, report it with the busy threshold, and say yes or no to whether the GPU is above that threshold.
Report whether the GPU is holding its clocks down right now, and the reason: heat, power limit, or being idle.
Read used and total video memory from the latest live sample.
Rank processes by GPU load and video memory; per-process GPU use is not recorded, so the answer is the list of what ask can answer.
Take GPU temperature, load and video memory history in the window; GPU history is not recorded, so the answer is the list of what ask can answer.
Rank programs by GPU use in the window; per-process GPU history is not recorded, so the answer is the list of what ask can answer.
Report the CPU model, core and thread counts from the hardware identity record.
Report the GPU model and total video memory from the hardware identity record.
Report the total RAM size from the hardware identity record.
Report the disk model and size from the hardware identity record.
Report the running kernel version from the kernel identity record.
List the full hardware and kernel identity record: CPU, GPU, RAM, disk and kernel.
Report the distribution name, version and laptop model; these are not recorded, so the answer is the list of what ask can answer.
Report the current BIOS version and date and whether the power state allows a firmware flash (charger in, battery charged); the update file itself is not checked.
Which firmware (BIOS or UEFI) setup options are set or were changed: boot order, secure boot, the firmware's own fan and power modes; the firmware's settings are not read here and are not recorded.
reply: I don't record BIOS settings: the firmware's setup options (boot order, secure boot, its own fan and power modes) stay inside the firmware, outside what this machine logs. I can tell you the BIOS version and its date, and whether the power state allows a firmware update.

answer: Check every live reading against its threshold, along with open spike events, failed units and untrusted processes; say yes or no to whether anything is wrong, and list each problem with its culprit, most severe first.
Take all spike events, crashes, unit failures and failed trust checks in the window, order them by severity, and name the culprit of each.
List every recorded event in the window in time order: spikes, crashes, unit starts and failures, package and config changes, device changes and flashes.
Count the error messages in the system journal in the window, grouped by the program or service that wrote them, with an example message from each.
List every spike, crash, trust check and live-sample appearance for the named program in the window, in time order, with totals.
Compare the counts of spikes, crashes and unit failures in the window with the average of previous recorded periods, by type.
Group the spike events in the window by culprit and hour of day, and report the ones that happen on most days at about the same time.

Take the named program's runs that overlap the window, add up the time it was open (each run cut to the window), and report the total, the number of separate runs, and the longest run with its start and end.

Say whether the machine was used in the window and by whom: the records can't tell who; the log-ins, sleep and wake, the lid, the charger and the programs opened by hand (desktop apps and terminal tabs) show whether and when it was in use.
Which browser tabs, pages or websites are or were open, or visited; ask records programs and their processes, not what is inside them.
reply: I can't see browser tabs, pages or the sites you visited: I record programs and their processes, not what is inside them. I can tell you whether the browser is running now, when it ran, and how much CPU and memory it used.

answer: What was typed, written, said or shown on screen; keystrokes, text and screen contents are not recorded.
reply: I don't record what you type or what is on the screen: no keystrokes, text or screenshots. I can tell you which programs were running at that moment and what the machine was doing (CPU, heat, memory), or why it shut off.

answer: Requests to remind, alert or schedule something for later; ask answers questions from the records and does not run on a schedule or act later.
reply: I can't set reminders or alarms: I only answer questions about this machine from its records, and I don't run in the background to act later. A calendar or reminder app can do that.

answer: Say that this is outside what the records hold and list what ask can answer.
reply: That's outside what this machine's records hold. I can answer about temperature and heat, CPU load, memory, disk activity, network traffic, battery, the GPU, what runs at startup, updates, crashes, devices plugged in, whether a program is known, and what the hardware is.
